signals.title: Introducing Kinference: An Open Source Inference Control Plane for vLLM and Kubernetes | vLLM Blog
signals.excerpt:
# Introducing Kinference: An Open Source Inference Control Plane for vLLM and Kubernetes

November 4, 2026 7 min read

Table of Contents

We’re excited to announce Kinference [kay-inference], a new open source project for building scalable inference platforms with vLLM.

Kinference by Buoyant

We created Kinference at Buoyant after watching our customers struggle to run open weight models in their environments. We designed Kinference to be the control plane layer for the platform you need to build. It uses vLLM to do the underlying inference, and provides the set of features necessary for building an inference platform in practice. This includes token rate limiting, tenant usage and cost tracking, intelligent load balancing, and inference policies.

...

In addition to policies and a routing layer, Kinference provides inference-specific load balancing that takes into account signals like GPU queue sizes, historical performance, and the contents of the KV cache on the GPU. This KV-cache awareness, in particular, allows Kinference to send requests to the vLLM worker that will do the least work for that specific request.

Modeling the KV cache content of the GPU can produce dramatic gains in performance for distributed inference. For example, in our public Kinference benchmarks, we showed that, when compared to standard Kubernetes load balancing (labeled “service” below), Kinference (labeled “kinference”) was able to cut median time-to-first-token (TTFT) by 95% and median end-to-end latency by 45% of requests on one workload type.

...

In the capacity benchmark, Kinference served 7.4× the goodput on shared-prefix and about 3.5× the goodput on multiturn. It was able to attain our chosen SLO at concurrency 32 (the highest measured) on our shared-prefix workload, and concurrency 8 on the multiturn workload, whereas the kube-proxy approach was not able to attain the SLO at any concurrency level.

...

Feedback, issues and benchmark reports from other deployments are very welcome.

signals.title: Cohere Makes Embed 5 and Rerank 5 Available on OpenRouter | AI.info
signals.excerpt:
AI.info Team · Written with AI · fact-checked · 2026-11-05

Cohere says Embed 5 and Rerank 5 are now live on OpenRouter, with access through a single API. Its demonstration builds a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline, which retrieves relevant text from a document collection before a language model answers a question.

## One OpenRouter key for retrieval and generation

OpenRouter users can use the same API key and credits they already use for other models, with no additional setup. Cohere’s walkthrough uses one client for embedding documents, retrieving candidates, reranking them and sending selected text to a chat model. The workflow needs no separate SDKs, accounts or bills to manage.

The pipeline has an offline indexing stage and an online path that runs for each question. Indexing embeds document chunks to make them searchable; each question then calls an Embed 5 Fast model, a Rerank 5 model and a chat model through OpenRouter’s API. Cohere frames knowing which calls happen once and which happen per request as a way to explain most of the pipeline’s cost and latency.

...

The walkthrough’s retrieval function requests up to 20 chunks by cosine similarity. Its sample corpus contains six documents, each producing one chunk, so the example can return at most six candidates. Rerank 5 then re-scores the candidates, returns up to five, and the sample code drops any result with a relevance score below 0.3. Fewer than five results may therefore remain. Cohere describes Rerank 5’s scores as calibrated across queries and domains, so the same relevance threshold can filter weak context before it reaches the language model.

Rerank 5 can score a query and chunk together with up to 32,000 tokens combined; the walkthrough says longer inputs are split into several passes. Cohere says it reranks semi-structured material such as JSON records and tables well when formatted as YAML strings, and that switching rerank models does not require re-indexing because reranking reads raw text at query time. The post recommends Rerank 5 Pro for reasoning-heavy queries and long or domain-specific documents, and Rerank 5 Fast for high-volume search and agents that search many times per task.

...

Once reranking selects the chunks, the sample sends them as numbered sources to a chat model and asks it to answer from those sources alone. The example uses deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017, while its code comment says any chat model on OpenRouter can fill that role. If no result clears the relevance threshold, the sample skips the language-model call.

signals.excerpt:
# AMD releases online quantization for vLLM ATOM SGLang

AMD has introduced online quantization, a feature that quantizes model weights layer by layer during the model-loading stage inside serving engines rather than ahead of time through a separate export job. This approach eliminates the need for intermediate disk checkpoints and enables fast exploration of quantization schemes, dynamic requantization, and reinforcement learning rollouts. Integrations are available in inference engines including vLLM, ATOM, and SGLang, with benchmarks showing that online quantization matches the accuracy and latency of traditional offline methods. signals.title: Supercharging XLA-based inference: Announcing the launch of XLA Serving Engine | Google Open Source Blog
signals.excerpt:
#### Thursday, November 5, 2026

Oleg Shaldybin

 and 

Monica Song

, Google TPU Software

Today we are excited to announce the launch of XLA Serving Engine (XSE), a general-purpose model export and inference runtime for the OpenXLA ecosystem, open-sourced under the Apache 2.0 license.

We created XLA Serving Engine to enable a “Train in Python, Serve in C++” workflow. Most ML engineers develop models using Python (with frameworks like JAX and PyTorch); however, some production serving environments do not allow Python due to operational and deployment complexity. XLA Serving Engine offers a solution by providing an API for engineers to export their ML models to an “XLA SavedModel” containing the StableHLO representation of their model’s function, which can then be loaded and executed by the XLA Serving Runtime.

This approach allows users to serve models (typically non-LLMs) directly in a C++ runtime, which enables high throughput at any scale and optimizes for low latency by removing the overhead of the Python interpreter. In our studies, we found that for short requests, XSE delivers 2–5x the throughput of the best Python server we could build, and 8–36x that of a straightforward one, while using 30–70% less CPU time per prediction and a quarter of the memory.

Last year, we began deploying core components of XLA Serving Engine as part of Google’s internal load-bearing, production serving infrastructure. Today, XSE serves over 6 million queries per second and powers some of Google's highest-volume online inference pipelines, including YouTube Shorts, Google Ads, Search, and parts of Gemini Omni, with plans to onboard more customers internally.

...

- Python-Free Serving: XSE enables a “Train in Python, Serve in C++” workflow via the intermediary compiled XLA SavedModel serialization format. In our studies, we found that XSE delivers 2–5x the throughput of a pure Python server.
- Low-latency execution: The XLA Serving Runtime wraps PJRT directly and optimizes the model using the XLA compiler. This eliminates Python runtime overhead and the global interpreter lock. XSE is C++ native, which means one process is capable of using all eight cores.

...

- Orbax Checkpointing Integration: XLA SavedModel stores JAX model computations as StableHLO and uses Orbax checkpoint to store the weights.
- Flexible Scale: Supports both single-host and multi-host serving by leveraging PJRT.
- Performance Parity: XSE preserves the performance of the model’s forward function (including kernel optimizations). Hand off your model to XLA Serving Engine with confidence that performance will be identical to its training environment.
- Docker Packages: We provide a suite of Docker images that are tested on CPU, GPU, and TPU and expose simple gRPC APIs for calling your model.

signals.excerpt:
# Kimi K3.1 Pro on AMD Instinct GPUs: Day-0 support and optimization

 Nov 04, 2026

# TL;DR

- Kimi K3.1 Pro, Moonshot AI’s open-weight, natively multimodal agentic model (2.8T total and 104B activated parameters, 1M-token context), serves on 8× AMD Instinct™ MI355X GPUs with both ATOM and vLLM on day 0, from the released MXFP4 checkpoint and with its DSpark speculative-decoding draft.
- K3.1 Pro keeps Kimi K3’s hybrid architecture: 69 Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) layers and 24 latent-attention layers over an 896-expert MXFP4 MoE. It adds a sparse indexer (DSA) to every one of the 24 attention layers, which selects 2,048 tokens of history per query. ATOM serves the indexed layers on its shared DSA path, with an FP8 index cache next to the FP8 latent KV cache
- ATOM: native KDA and sparse MLA kernels, the routed experts on FlyDSL’s MXFP4 grouped MoE, per-channel FP8 attention applied at start-up, and a DSpark draft that shares the target’s KV cache and runs as a captured CUDA graph.
- vLLM: memory-efficient sparse attention with decode context parallelism (DCP) for long-context serving, alongside a specialized decode path for low-latency interactive workloads
- Accuracy on Moonshot AI’s Kimi Vendor Verifier, at reasoning effort max: OCRBench 0.871 (Moonshot reference 0.872); tool-call JSON schema 0.991.

...

# Serving with ATOM

ATOM serves Kimi K3.1 Pro with tensor parallelism over the eight GPUs of one MI355X node, for text and image input, from the released MXFP4 checkpoint without conversion. With the DSpark draft loaded, each GPU peaks at about 199 GB of its 288 GB during start-up, and a single 1M-token request fits on one node.

...

PTPC FP8 attention: At start-up, ATOM re-quantizes the BF16 attention and dense linears to FP8 with one scale per output channel, with activations scaled per token at run time (--online_quant_config with ptpc_fp8): 559 linears per rank, done in about 2 seconds. The routed experts, the KDA convolutions, the vision encoder and the indexer-packed down-projection keep their stored formats.

...

vLLM supports Kimi K3.1 Pro on AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs with the MXFP4 checkpoint and DSpark speculative decoding. Built on AITER and FlyDSL kernels, the ROCm implementation combines memory-efficient sparse attention with decode context parallelism (DCP) for long-context serving, alongside a specialized decode path for low-latency interactive workloads.

signals.title: Box taps Nvidia’s Nemotron for new agent-first content retrieval system | TechCrunch
signals.excerpt:
At its developer conference on Thursday, Box showed off a new feature that will build Nvidia’s Nemotron embedding system into the core of its product. 

Called Box Content Retrieval, the new feature allows agents to answer queries far more effectively by relying on the embedded metadata created by Nemotron. 

Box says the upshot for users is faster, more accurate, and less expensive queries. Nvidia’s VP of generative AI software, Kari Briski, told TechCrunch that she expects queries to be answered four times faster, with 20% fewer errors and 90% fewer tokens used.

The system will be available to all of Box’s Enterprise Advance customers, rolling out early next year.

“This dramatically boosts both the relevance of our search technology for agents,” Box CEO Aaron Levie said. “Instead of an agent having to kind of read through each document, we can send back chunks from the documents that are most relevant to the user’s query or whatever the task is that the agent is doing.”

The feature is an implementation of Nvidia’s Nemotron Embed project, which offers open-weight embedding models to improve automated retrieval systems. Major labs have often overlooked such models, which use LLMs to pre-process data so it can be better used by agents. The sector has been a focus for Nvidia’s open source model project, with its recent Nemotron release in July topping the RTEB benchmark, which measures retrieval quality.

The system will be most useful when paired with active agents, Box says, giving the example of lawyers, who will ostensibly be able to find relevant clauses and precedents more easily under the new system. Because Nemotron’s embeddings go beyond simple keywords to map underlying concepts, a search tool can surface related legal themes even when different wording or language is used.

While the Nemotron models are freely available, the system also relies heavily on Box’s pre-existing metadata and permission controls, which will make it challenging to recreate from scratch. “We’re probably packing in five different technologies into one simple API,” Levie told TechCrunch.

signals.title: vLLM Delivers Day-0 Support for Kimi K3.1 Pro | vLLM Blog
signals.excerpt:
# vLLM Delivers Day-0 Support for Kimi K3.1 Pro

November 4, 2026 22 min read

Table of Contents

Kimi K3.1 Pro is Moonshot AI's most capable open-weight model: a 2.8T-parameter (104B active) multimodal MoE with a 1M-token context that matches the strongest closed-source models on coding, agentic and knowledge benchmarks.

The main change is attention: K3.1 Pro adds Sparse Attention (DSA) to all 24 full-attention layers for efficiency. vLLM supports it on day 0 on NVIDIA GPUs, AMD GPUs, Google TPUs and Alibaba T-Head Zhenwu PPUs.

## TL;DR

- Sparse attention on a hybrid model: K3.1 Pro keeps K3's KDA + MLA hybrid and adds a DSA indexer to all 24 MLA layers. At long context, a decode step reads about a quarter of the bytes per layer that dense MLA reads.
- One KV cache for three kinds of state: vLLM packs each block's MLA latent, indexer keys and KDA state together. The packed cache runs with FlashInfer and FlashMLA sparse kernels with FP8 or NVFP4 KV and optional MXFP4 index keys, and P/D disaggregation transfers it unchanged.
- Token-sharded prefill attention: up to 1.69× faster time to first token (TTFT) than head-sharded prefill at 340K tokens on 8× GB300.
- Decode context parallelism (DCP) with a sparse indexer: an exact top-k merge with ~10× less traffic makes the attention module 1.3–1.5× faster at DCP8. DCP prefill attention runs 4.1–4.3× faster per layer, and DCP8 holds 7.2× the KV tokens of TP8.
- Fused low-latency decode: the specialized CuTe DSL decode path from Kimi K3 now covers DSA layers, making decode 1.2–1.6× faster on 8× GB300, and 1.9× faster under DCP8.
- Agentic serving: on NVIDIA GB300, up to 375.9 tok/s per user at the latency-sensitive end and 37.8K total tok/s per GPU at the throughput end; on NVIDIA Rubin, up to 815.6 tok/s per user and 68.7K total tok/s per GPU on the SemiAnalysis AgentX benchmark.
- Zero-mismatch RL on day 0: for the first time, day-0 support comes with zero-mismatch RL: vLLM and Megatron produce bit-identical log-probs for both the base model and the LoRA adapter, so the PPO KL is exactly 0 at every step of a 100-step full-model run.

...

vLLM delivers strong performance on agentic serving workloads. We benchmark our day-0 image with the SemiAnalysis AgentX benchmark on NVIDIA GB300 and NVIDIA Rubin.

### NVIDIA GB300

At the latency-sensitive end of the frontier, Kimi K3.1 Pro holds 375.9 tokens per second per user. Further along the frontier, it keeps each user above 100 tokens per second while serving 19.2K total tokens per second per GPU. At the throughput end, it reaches 37.8K tokens per second per GPU, about 26× the most interactive point, while each user still sees about 54 tokens per second.

Figure 7: AgentX Pareto frontier for Kimi K3.1 Pro on NVIDIA GB300, with 4 speculative tokens and a synthetic acceptance length of 3.36 tokens. Hover a point for its configuration and metrics.

### NVIDIA Rubin

On NVIDIA Rubin, Kimi K3.1 Pro holds 815.6 tokens per second per user at the latency-sensitive end of the frontier. Further along the frontier, it keeps each user above 100 tokens per second while serving 46.0K total tokens per second per GPU. At the throughput end, it reaches 68.7K tokens per second per GPU, about 51× the most interactive point, while each user still sees about 75 tokens per second.

signals.title: Leveling the Playing Field: Building a 100% Offline Kubernetes Docs RAG Exam Assistant with Web AI, Gemma 4, and WebGPU - DEV Community
signals.excerpt:
In this article, we'll walk through the architecture and implementation of Kubernetes WebAI RAG—an open-source, 100% offline Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system running entirely inside the browser using Gemma 4 E2B, EmbeddingGemma, LiteRT-LM, TensorFlow.js, and WebGPU.

...

This project builds upon Jason Mayes' `VectorSearch.js`, which pioneered client-side vector similarity search in the browser using TensorFlow.js and WebGPU.

To transform a general-purpose browser vector search demo into an exam-ready Kubernetes Q&A system, we re-engineered the workflow around a core principle: Prepare once on the maintainer's machine; run identically and offline on every student's browser.

Key architectural upgrades in `kubernetes-webai-rag` include:

- Zero Startup Indexing: Instead of scraping or embedding documents in the student's browser (which would take hours) or importing massive payloads into IndexedDB on page load, the maintainer prebuilds a normalized 16,483-chunk float32 vector matrix (`768` dimensions) alongside a BM25 inverted keyword index.
- Hybrid Search with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF): Combines semantic understanding (`EmbeddingGemma`) with exact Kubernetes terminology matching (`BM25`), grouping by headings and enforcing page diversity.
- Bundled Local Documentation Mirror: Strips external scripts, rewrites links, and mirrors the entire readable Kubernetes documentation snapshot locally so students can verify every `[1]`, `[2]` citation side-by-side.
- On-Device Generation with Gemma 4 E2B & LiteRT-LM: Streams grounded answers and YAML manifests directly from the student's GPU, backed by atomic Origin Private File System (OPFS) model caching.

...

### 1. Concept Retrieval & Real-Time Streaming 

When a student asks a question (e.g., "What is a Pod in Kubernetes and how do I create a Deployment?"), the app:

- Embeds only the question (plus up to 2 recent user questions for follow-up context) on-device using `EmbeddingGemma`.
- Searches all 16,483 prebuilt chunks in milliseconds using WebGPU matrix multiplication and BM25 keyword search.
- Streams a grounded explanation from Gemma 4 E2B with inline citations like `[1]`, `[2]`.

signals.title: Building Private Offline RAG in Pure Python: Ollama, SQLite-Vec & Function Calling Agents - DEV Community
signals.excerpt:
Posted on Nov 3 

# Building Private Offline RAG in Pure Python: Ollama, SQLite-Vec & Function Calling Agents 

Paying metered per-million-token bills to OpenAI or Anthropic is killing AI startup margins in 2026. If your application handles 10,000 queries per day with multi-turn context and reasoning models, you are bleeding between $800 and $3,000 every single month in variable API costs. Furthermore, healthcare, legal, and enterprise clients flatly refuse to allow sensitive internal documents to cross public cloud network boundaries.

In this deep architectural breakdown, we will build a 100% private, zero-cloud RAG pipeline and autonomous agent engine in pure Python. It runs entirely on local hardware, costs $0.00 in ongoing API subscription fees, and operates with sub-millisecond local vector retrieval.

## 1. High-Level Architecture: Zero-Cloud Local AI 

Here is the operational pipeline: 

```
[User Query / Document Input]
              ↓
  [Local Embedding Model: nomic-embed-text / bge-m3]
              ↓
  [Single-File Serverless Vector DB: SQLite + BLOB Math]
  (Cosine Similarity via NumPy or sqlite-vec)
              ↓
  [Top-K Semantic Context Assembly + Prompt Guardrails]
              ↓
  [Local Reasoning Model: Ollama / DeepSeek-R1 / Qwen 2.5]
  (Strict Deterministic JSON Extraction via Pydantic V2)
              ↓
  [Autonomous Tool Execution / Structured Response]

```

...

## 4. Deterministic Structured Tool Calling with Pydantic V2 

Local models (like `qwen2.5-coder:7b` or `deepseek-r1:8b`) can execute real-world tools with 100% syntactic reliability when paired with Ollama's `format="json"` and Pydantic schema validation: 

```
# app/agents/tool_caller.py
import json
import ollama
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class DatabaseQueryIntent(BaseModel):
    action: str = Field(description="Query action: select, insert, or update")
    table_name: str = Field(description="Target table name")
    filters: dict = Field(default_factory=dict, description="Query filters")
    limit: int = Field(default=10, description="Max rows to return")

async def parse_user_command(user_prompt: str) -> DatabaseQueryIntent:
    client = ollama.AsyncClient()
    schema = DatabaseQueryIntent.model_json_schema()

    system_prompt = (
        "You are an autonomous command parser. "
        "Convert user intent into the following JSON schema strictly:\n"
        f"{json.dumps(schema)}\n"
        "Return ONLY raw valid JSON. No conversational preamble."
    )

    response = await client.chat(
        model="qwen2.5-coder:7b",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": system_prompt},
            {"role": "user", "content": user_prompt}
        ],
        format="json"
    )

    raw_json = response["message"]["content"]
    return DatabaseQueryIntent(**json.loads(raw_json))

signals.title: NVIDIA Boosts Ling-3.0-flash Throughput 42.5% On DGX Spark - Dataconomy
signals.excerpt:
NVIDIA said three software optimizations raised decode throughput for Ant Group inclusionAI’s Ling-3.0-flash model by 42.5% on a single DGX Spark desktop system.

Tests across all 1,319 GSM8K questions increased throughput to 53.89 tokens per second from 37.81 tokens per second, while accuracy changed to 96.82% from 96.89%, a statistically undetectable difference, NVIDIA said.

The test used Ling-3.0-flash-fp4, a mixture-of-experts model with 124 billion total parameters and 5.1 billion active parameters per token. The model has a native 256,000-token context window.

DGX Spark uses NVIDIA’s GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip and has 128 GB of unified memory and 273 GB/s of memory bandwidth. NVIDIA rates the system for inference on models with as many as 200 billion parameters and says it can deliver up to 1 petaFLOP of sparse FP4 computing performance.

NVIDIA profiled the model at batch size one and found decoding was constrained by memory reads, particularly in mixture-of-experts computation and the language-model output head. The baseline followed the official W4A8 recipe, using FlashInfer MXFP4 MoE kernels, CUTLASS dense GEMM and an FP32 language-model head.

...

The first change replaced FlashInfer’s MoE backend with Humming, an independent kernel library that compiles kernels at runtime for specific matrix shapes, data types and GPUs. NVIDIA said the change supported the model’s narrow 768-wide expert layer and increased throughput by 9.3% to 39.45 tokens per second.

The second change applied FP8 quantization to the language-model head at load time. The head is a 157,184-by-2,560 BF16 matrix, and NVIDIA said FP8 halves the memory reads required for that layer. Humming combined with the FP8 head reached 43.94 tokens per second, up 21.7% from baseline.

The third change used multi-token prediction speculative decoding through Ling-3.0-flash’s built-in NEXTN prediction layer, eliminating the need for a separate draft model. On the synthetic test, 3.90 tokens were accepted per round and throughput rose to 102.88 tokens per second, a 185.1% increase from baseline.

...

With all three changes enabled on GSM8K, time per output token fell to 18.56 milliseconds from 26.45 milliseconds. Mean latency declined 24.5% to 11.49 seconds from 15.21 seconds.

Published 11/4/2026

# Together Compiler: Continual Compilation for AI inference

- Authors Reyna Abhyankar, Dylan Lim, and Simran Arora
- Table of contents 40+ Models Chosen for Production...40+ Models Chosen for Production...40+ Models Chosen for Production...
- Links in this article Polymorphic Inference Paper

AI inference workloads are dynamic. There are thousands of regimes spanning new models, hardware platforms, customers, use cases, and traffic shapes. It’s no longer scalable to optimize each of these regimes by hand.

...

Agents are a great fit for this problem, in theory. They can adapt to new workloads and search over the space of possible optimizations without relying on fixed rules or heuristics that plague human experts and traditional machine learning compilers. However, today’s agentic systems are bottlenecked by the speed of experimentation.

### We introduce Together Compiler (TKCC), the first truly continual RSI system that leverages high-throughput agents to optimize to diverse inference workloads.

In less than 24 hours, TKCC achieves up to 2.6x higher TPS across frontier open source models (Kimi K3, GLM 5.3, MiniMax M3.1-Flash, DeepSeek v4.1-Flash), sets the state-of-the-art on SemiAnalysis’ InferenceX benchmark for low-latency with 1111 TPS on MiniMax M3.1-Flash and 1205 TPS on DeepSeek v4.1-Flash, and outperforms available open-source megakernels by 1.7x on their workhorse Llama 1B batch size 1 setting. Furthermore, TKCC generalizes to domains beyond language model inference (weather modeling, PDE, time-series, and biology). This performance boost is enabled by TKCC’s 252x higher experiment throughput compared to baseline agentic RSI performance optimization systems. Together Compiler is serving trillions of tokens today.

...

## Overview of Together Compiler

TKCC takes as input the traffic shape, model, and hardware. TKCC uses agents to generate a series of optimizations for an inference engine. 

Figure 1: Together Compiler recompiles as traffic drifts, with agents, a persistent engine and an ensemble in a loop.

### The core insights in TKCC are as follows:

1. TKCC maximizes experimentation throughput and minimizes GPU idle time during agent optimization

‍ Most existing agentic inference optimization systems require agents to launch and teardown engines like VLLM, SGLang, or TRT-LLM to test each new experiment. However, engine start times are tens of minutes, significantly impeding experimentation throughput (see table below). Instead, TKCC proposes a new paradigm of “persistent engines” where the engine starts up once and can hot-reload any candidate forward pass, without any restarts. To ensure that the persistent engines constantly have new optimizations to test, TKCC spawns multiple agents that continually generate ideas and communicate via a message board to parallelize their efforts.

...

We select popular open-source code bases across weather modeling, PDE, time-series, and biology. We show the geometric mean speedups of TKCC over simply using Claude Code with the /goal command, illustrating that the principles of TKCC generalize across domains. We have been using TKCC as a general purpose AI compiler beyond LLM inference.

signals.title: Open-source AI this week: Humming kernels and vLLM on TPUs
signals.excerpt:
vLLM shipped Humming, a quantized-kernel library built with Ant Group, and vllm-torchtpu, a Google Cloud TPU backend, alongside day-0 model support.

...

The vLLM project, the open-source engine many teams use to serve language models, shipped two notable pieces of infrastructure over the past two weeks: Humming, a library of fast kernels for quantized models built with Ant Group, and `vllm-torchtpu`, a backend that runs vLLM on Google Cloud TPUs. It also kept up its habit of day-0 support for new models, including Mistral Large 4 on October 29. This edition covers what each release does, the numbers the maintainers published, and the caveats.

## Humming: one description of quantization, many fast kernels

Quantization shrinks a model’s weights, and sometimes its activations, to fewer bits so it fits in less memory and runs faster. The catch is that every format needs a matching GPU kernel, and writing them one by one does not scale. Humming, announced October 21, separates the description of a quantized computation from the choice of how to execute it. A unified representation turns different export formats into one description of weights, scales and zero points, and kernels are compiled just in time from shared CUDA components.

...

Per the project’s post, it supports weight-and-activation combinations from W4A16 to W4A4, formats such as INT4, MXFP4, MXINT4 and NVFP4, and NVIDIA GPUs from Turing onward, plus T-Head’s Zhenwu 810E. The authors credit engineers from Ant Group and the vLLM community.

The reported results are community microbenchmarks, with baselines that vary by chart:

- Dense W4A16 matches or beats vLLM’s Marlin kernels in most tested settings, with larger gains on some B300 cases.
- For mixture-of-experts layers, MXFP4 reaches about twice Marlin on H20 and H200 at medium and large batches.
- In one end-to-end test on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with eight H20 GPUs, switching from Marlin W4A16 to Humming W4A8 raised output throughput by 14% to 43% and cut mean time to first token by about 25% to 32%.

...

Marlin is the established open kernel for 4-bit weights in vLLM; Humming targets a wider range of formats and GPU generations rather than one format. The honest reading is “promising, verify on your hardware.” The post itself notes limits: autotuning is not yet available so heuristics may miss the best configuration on some workloads, the end-to-end test covers one model on one setup, and it names no license in the text we reviewed, so check the repository before adopting. For background, see our quantization explainer.

## vllm-torchtpu: vLLM on Google TPUs

Announced October 20, `vllm-torchtpu` is an out-of-tree platform plugin that vLLM detects automatically once installed. It builds on Google’s TorchTPU stack and comes from a partnership between Inferact and Google. The goal is to keep the same CLI, OpenAI-compatible server, scheduler and KV cache manager that users have on GPUs, so most supported models should serve on TPU without model-code changes.

Key details from the post:

- TPU v7x (Ironwood) is the recommended target and is tested in continuous integration on every pull request; v6e, v5e and v5p are experimental.
- Custom Pallas kernels cover attention variants, fused mixture-of-experts and quantized matrix multiplies in FP8, INT8, MXFP4 and NVFP4.
- All six of vLLM’s parallelism dimensions work across multi-host TPU slices, and the backend supports KV cache offloading to host memory and disaggregated prefill and decode.
- Installation is `pip install vllm-torchtpu` on a Cloud TPU VM with Python 3.12; the first start compiles graphs, which can take minutes.

...

- Humming is a quantized-kernel library from Ant Group and the vLLM community, available in vLLM 0.29.0.
- Maintainer benchmarks show up to roughly 2x over Marlin on some mixture-of-experts layers, with caveats.
- `vllm-torchtpu` runs vLLM on Google Cloud TPUs, with v7x as the supported target.
- No TPU performance numbers have been published yet.
- Validate vendor and community benchmarks on your own workload.

signals.title: Baidu Releases ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base for Further Training – Unite.AI
signals.excerpt:
Baidu’s ERNIE Team announced ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base on November 5, 2026, releasing downloadable weights for a text-only mixture-of-experts model with 280 billion total parameters and 14 billion activated per token. The checkpoint ends pre-training, before mid-training or post-training, giving developers a common starting point for domain adaptation, instruction tuning and reinforcement-learning research.

The release also provides a fixed baseline for controlled comparisons of training methods. Baidu said a post-trained ERNIE 5.5 Flash model will follow this base version.

...

## Baidu’s Benchmark Results

Baidu evaluated ERNIE against the publicly released DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base, Hy3-preview-Base and MiMo-V2.5-Base checkpoints with the same harness, prompts and few-shot examples, and the same LLM judge for free-form question answering. Selected results from its table show where the model leads and where it trails:

| Benchmark | ERNIE 5.5 Flash | DeepSeek V4 Flash | Hy3 preview | MiMo V2.5 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| MMLU, five-shot EM | 93.3 | 89.4 | 87.5 | 87.6 |
| HumanEval+, one-shot Pass@1 | 82.3 | 69.5 | 78.0 | 74.4 |
| FullStackBench, one-shot Pass@1 | 54.6 | 43.3 | 56.7 | 54.1 |
| InfiniteBench, zero-shot average | 46.5 | 48.0 | 33.0 | 46.7 |

Baidu’s comparison is task-dependent rather than a clean sweep: ERNIE leads the MMLU and HumanEval+ results shown, while Hy3 leads FullStackBench and DeepSeek leads InfiniteBench. The table supports strong exam and coding showings within Baidu’s evaluation while preserving those exceptions.

...

Downloads are available in FP8 and BF16 safetensors formats. The model card documents production serving with SGLang and vLLM through the completions API, matching the checkpoint’s base-model status. NVIDIA’s Megatron Bridge recipe adds a supervised fine-tuning workflow covering data preparation, training and export back to Hugging Face format. Its full-model recipe uses 16 nodes with four GB300 GPUs per node. NVIDIA validates the recipes on Blackwell GB200 and GB300 systems; the components support Hopper, but Hopper is not validated.

signals.title: Introducing AgentEnv: An Open-Source Framework for Building RL Environments | Scale Labs
signals.excerpt:
10/5/2026

# Introducing AgentEnv: An Open-Source Framework for Building RL Environments

By Edgar Arakelyan, Tejas Polakam, Yzabelle Go

An agent is only as good as the world it operates in, and building worlds that are realistic, accurate, and scalable all at once is the hard part of scaling RL. Every RL environment Scale builds runs on AgentEnv. Today we're open-sourcing it.

...

Most tools for agent training start from the task and build a world around it. AgentEnv’s philosophy starts from the world first, so one Environment can host many Tasks and many agents. AgentEnv is built on two core principles

Building blocks: What an Environment is made of. An Environment is built from versioned composable blocks: Environments like Slack or Gmail, an Artifact of data that populates them, and Rules (the clock, triggers, and roles) that govern how it behaves.

Interoperability: What an Environment works with. An Environment doesn't assume anything about who or what runs it. Any agent can connect to it, any sandbox can host it, and your cloud can run it, all through open protocols instead of custom glue.

...

#### Designed for Interoperability

Agent Agnostic. An Environment's card tells an agent which tools it serves and how to reach them, over MCP, REST or a generated CLI. An agent's Agent Card, from the open A2A protocol, does the same in the other direction.

Pair any Environment Card with any Agent Card and the agent can start work, with no custom wiring. The same Task runs unchanged and consistent on Claude Code, OpenAI's agents, or any of your own custom agents.

...

In the future, we will be adding

...

A Task is constructed as a DAG of AgentEnv steps. Each step represents a primitive action on an Agent, the Environment and more, like setting up the world, loading data, setting the clock, bringing in an agent, handing it the work, collecting what it made, grading the result with a rubric or a strict check.

...

### What comes out of the box

AgentEnv ships 48 built-in step types, covering everything from deploying an Environment to setting its Rules of the World to grading trajectories. Most RL Tasks can be built from these alone, with no new code. For the rest, you can add your own steps as plugins.

signals.title: 4-Bit Quantization Drops Video Quality on AMD GPUs
signals.excerpt:
By AI Daily Post Edited by Brian Petersen, Editor-in-Chief November 4, 2026 • 4 min read 

AMD's ROCm team ran a quantization experiment on Wan2.2-T2V-A14B, a large diffusion transformer used for text-to-video generation, and found that shrinking every layer to 4-bit weights and 4-bit activations produces a visible quality drop, even when the VBench score looks close to the full-precision BF16 baseline. Full W4A4 MXFP4 quantization scored 0.8520 on VBench overall. That's a small numerical gap from BF16, but the blog's authors say the gap shows up clearly in the generated video itself.

The fix they tested isn't quantizing everything the same way. Using AMD Quark, the team evaluated each transformer block individually and promoted only the blocks sensitive to precision loss from W4A4 to W4A8, leaving the rest on the cheaper 4-bit path. That calibration-driven mix pushed the score to 0.8648. A separate test quantizing the entire model to W4A8 using round-to-nearest (RTN) hit 0.8658, the highest quantized score measured in the study, suggesting FP8 activations applied model-wide can close most of the quality loss on their own.

All the W4A8 figures here come from quantize-dequantize emulation, not live hardware execution, so this is a quality study rather than a speed benchmark. Native W4A8 runs are supported starting in AMD Quark 0.13.

> The safest reading is that full W4A8 and fixed-rotation/SmoothQuant-selected W4A8 are both near-BF16 quality, while the selected policy is the more practical current path because it uses W4A8 only where calibration indicates a benefit.
> 
> Quark Mixed-Precision Quantization for Wan2.2 Video Generation on AMD Instinct GPUs - AMD ROCm AI Blog

signals.title: Introducing Physical-Engineering’s Last Exam for agents
signals.excerpt:
November 3, 2026

Authors: Burak Gokturk, VP Research & Development; Rujun Han, Research Scientist; George Lee, Product Manager.

Today, the Google AI & Infrastructure team is announcing Physical-Engineering's Last Exam (PLE), a new benchmark and open competition, developed in collaboration with Mercor, and built to test a frontier model’s ability to complete tasks in mechanical, electrical, civil and structural engineering. 

To help the research community measure and improve how agents handle physical engineering work, we are releasing 29 public tasks, their grading tools, and an open competition leaderboard at ple-bench.com.

...

PLE closes this evaluation gap with 85 long-horizon tasks across four core disciplines: mechanical (30 tasks), electrical (27 tasks), civil (18 tasks), and structural (10 tasks) engineering.

Close this modal

Instead of answering a single prompt, an agent works inside a containerized project folder — built on Mercor’s Archipelago environment — that mirrors what a practicing engineer receives on the job. Each task holds an average of 61 files (5,170 total files across the benchmark), including PDFs, spreadsheets, emails, 2D CAD drawings, 3D BIM models, and document revisions. The agent must reason through these files, find the governing building codes and physical limits, run calculations, and generate production-ready deliverables that a licensed reviewer would review and approve.

...

### All frontier models score below 50%

We tested 14 frontier models on PLE using seven publicly available agent harnesses (Antigravity, Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, OpenCode, OpenHands, and Pi). Because PLE evaluates both code compliance and cost efficiency, agents only earn points if their design passes every hard safety check first. Our baseline results show a wide gap between current models and real-world engineering requirements:

- High headroom: All frontier models score below 50% on our private test set, with the highest-performing model on its native harness reaching a mean score of 48.3%.
- Hard safety gates: While the top-scoring agent configuration satisfied 91% of individual constraints on co-authored tasks, only 41.3% of its deliverables passed every hard safety and feasibility check required.
- Model vs. harness impact: Choice of model drives performance far more than the harness (up to a 50-point spread across models, versus a median 3-point spread across harnesses for the same model), though harnesses significantly affect run cost.

signals.title: Unified Brain Replaces Turn-Based LLM Agents with SQLite
signals.excerpt:
#### 💡 TL;DR

- DevLoops.ai released Unified Brain, an open-source framework that replaces conventional turn-based LLM agent communication with SQLite coordination.
- The system uses System One reasoning models and database-backed state management to eliminate sequential bottlenecks in multi-agent workflows.
- Unified Brain enables parallel agent execution and deterministic state tracking, addressing reliability issues in traditional agentic architectures.

DevLoops.ai has open-sourced Unified Brain, a framework that fundamentally rethinks how multiple LLM agents coordinate work. Instead of sequential turn-based communication where agents wait for each other to respond, the system uses SQLite as a shared coordination layer paired with System One reasoning models to enable parallel execution and deterministic state management.

...

Traditional LLM agent frameworks treat inter-agent communication like a chat conversation, with one agent speaking and others waiting. Unified Brain replaces this model with a database-centric architecture where agents query and update shared state through SQLite transactions. Each agent operates as an independent process that reads work items from the database, executes reasoning steps, and commits results atomically.

The framework leverages System One models, fast reasoning systems optimized for rapid inference, to handle coordination logic. This separation allows computationally expensive reasoning to happen in parallel across agents while the lightweight coordination layer manages task distribution and state synchronization through SQL queries.

## Release Date and Availability

Unified Brain was officially launched on November 3, 2026, with full source code available on GitHub under an open-source license. The initial release includes core coordination primitives, example agent implementations, and documentation for integrating custom reasoning models. DevLoops.ai positioned the launch as a community-driven effort to advance practical multi-agent system design.

...

The system uses SQLite's Write-Ahead Logging mode to support concurrent reads while maintaining ACID properties for state updates. Agents register tasks as database rows with status fields, and the coordination engine assigns work based on agent capabilities and current load. Failed tasks automatically retry with exponential backoff, and the database serves as an audit log for debugging agent behavior.

- Atomic state transitions prevent race conditions in task assignment
- SQL-based work queues eliminate custom message brokers
- Transaction logs enable deterministic replay of agent execution sequences
- Pluggable reasoning backends support both local and API-based models
